title: Matrices
summary: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers that lets us store and process data such as sales, prices or production in a compact form. This chapter covers types of matrices, equality, addition, scalar and matrix multiplication, transpose, symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices, and simple business applications.

notes.heading: Matrix, order and notation
notes.html:
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers (called elements or entries) arranged in rows and columns. A matrix with m rows and n columns has order m × n and has mn elements. We write A = [aij]m × n, where aij is the element in the i-th row and j-th column.

notes.heading: Types of matrices
notes.html:
• Row matrix: only one row (order 1 × n). Column matrix: only one column (order m × 1).
  • Square matrix: m = n. Its elements a11, a22, …, ann form the principal (leading) diagonal.
  • Diagonal matrix: a square matrix in which every non-diagonal element is 0.
  • Scalar matrix: a diagonal matrix with all diagonal elements equal (e.g. 5I).
  • Identity (unit) matrix I: a diagonal matrix with every diagonal element 1. AI = IA = A.
  • Zero (null) matrix O: every element is 0.
  • Upper / lower triangular matrix: all elements below / above the principal diagonal are 0.
  • Equal matrices: A = B when they have the same order and aij = bij for every i, j.

notes.heading: Operations on matrices
notes.html:
• Addition / subtraction: defined only for matrices of the same order; add or subtract corresponding elements. It is commutative (A + B = B + A) and associative.
  • Scalar multiplication: kA = [k aij] — multiply every element by k. k(A + B) = kA + kB.
  • Matrix multiplication: AB is defined only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. If A is m × n and B is n × p, then AB is m × p and (AB)ij = ai1b1j + ai2b2j + … + ainbnj ("row of A into column of B").
  • Multiplication is associative, A(BC) = (AB)C, and distributive, A(B + C) = AB + AC, but not commutative: in general AB ≠ BA.
  • AB = O does not imply A = O or B = O.
  • Powers: A2 = AA, A3 = A2A (only for square matrices).

notes.heading: Transpose; symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices
notes.html:
The transpose A′ (or AT) is obtained by interchanging rows and columns: if A is m × n then A′ is n × m and (A′)ij = aji.

  1. (A′)′ = A
  2. (kA)′ = kA′
  3. (A + B)′ = A′ + B′
  4. (AB)′ = B′A′ (reversal law)

A square matrix is symmetric if A′ = A (aij = aji) and skew-symmetric if A′ = −A (aij = −aji). Every diagonal element of a skew-symmetric matrix is 0, because aii = −aii.

Theorem. Every square matrix can be written uniquely as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix:

A = P + Q, where P = (A + A′)/2 is symmetric and Q = (A − A′)/2 is skew-symmetric.

Also, A + A′ is always symmetric and A − A′ is always skew-symmetric. The only matrix that is both symmetric and skew-symmetric is the zero matrix.

notes.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
notes.html:
• Multiplying corresponding elements (like addition) instead of "row into column".
  • Assuming AB = BA, or using (A + B)2 = A2 + 2AB + B2; the correct expansion is A2 + AB + BA + B2.
  • Writing (AB)′ = A′B′ instead of B′A′.
  • Trying to add matrices of different orders, or multiply when columns of A ≠ rows of B.
  • Writing the order as columns × rows; it is always rows × columns.
  • Forgetting that scalar multiplication multiplies every element (unlike a determinant, where k multiplies one row).

Case study. A school sells three kinds of tickets for its annual fair: Adult (₹100), Student (₹50) and Child (₹20). Sales over two days were:
Day 1: 120 adult, 300 student, 80 child tickets. Day 2: 150 adult, 250 student, 100 child tickets.
(i) Write the sales as a 2 × 3 matrix S and the prices as a 3 × 1 matrix P.
(ii) Find SP and interpret it.
(iii) If all prices are raised by 10%, use a matrix operation to find the new total collection over both days.
